newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASEAN, EU clear way for ties but can't agree on Burma, Timor.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN, EU clear way for ties but can't agree on Burma, Timor.

text.p: European and Southeast Asian nations had productive talks on Burma, East Timor and human rights issues on Thursday, but could not agree on how to deal with Rangoon's military government, a top official said.
Burma was scarcely mentioned in the draft of the final declaration the 22 ministers are expected to issue in Singapore on Friday.
"We had an exchange of views on Myanmar (Burma)," said the draft, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
The draft also made no reference to East Timor, although it once again was an issue on the sidelines.

Foreign ministers from the 15-member European Union (EU) and seven-member Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) talked for more than two hours on Burma alone, said conference chairman, Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar.
"This was one of the most productive and substantive discussions between the EU and ASEAN held to date," he said.
Jayakumar gave no details of the talks but suggested the gap between the two attitudes to Burma's military government had not changed.

"Not that each side has convinced the other. But both sides agreed that we now have, as a result of the dialogue, a better understanding of each other's insights, concerns and approaches on Myanmar (Burma)," he said.

The EU believes tough measures are needed to punish the Rangoon government for its crackdown on Burma's pro-democracy movement, while ASEAN believes "constructive engagement" will eventually coax the military regime to reform.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after a civil war followed Portugal's abrupt decolonisation of the territory. Up to a third of the population died in the famine and fighting that followed.
Indonesia annexed East Timor in 1976, but the United Nations still considers Portugal the administering power.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas accused Portugal of scuttling a more ambitious treaty that would redefine ties between the European nations and some of its former colonies into the next century.
"(East Timor) was one of the issues used by Portugal to prevent a new-generation agreement to be signed by the two sides and of course we deeply regret it," Alatas told reporters.
Portugal's Foreign Minister Jaime Gama said Lisbon had not vetoed the treaty but was merely insisting political and human rights issues be included.
Countries that did not want to include human rights issues in the treaty "are the ones who are putting the veto" on a new agreement, he told reporters.
The old agreement was signed in 1980, when the relationship was largely defined by aid from European nations to some of their former colonies in Asia.
A new treaty would outline dozens of new initiatives across the political, economic and cultural spectrum, according to a concept paper prepared by an Emminent Persons Group.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. All but Thailand are former European colonies.
A senior ASEAN official said such a new agreement would have the status of a treaty because it would require the signatures of all members.
The official said, however, many of the projects envisioned for the treaty would be included in the final declaration from this meeting.
"We can still have the substance, even without the form," the ASEAN official said.
